reason: Rich multi-source documentation verifies that a starquake on magnetar SGR 1806-20 blasted Earth's ionosphere from across the galaxy.
story: On December 27, 2004, the brightest cosmic blast ever recorded struck Earth. It originated halfway across the galaxy in Sagittarius from SGR 1806-20, an ultradense magnetar just twelve miles wide. Squeezed by a magnetic field of a thousand trillion gauss, the star's rigid crust fractured in a colossal starquake. In a tenth of a second, this rupture discharged more energy than our Sun produces in over 100,000 years. In gamma rays, the flash momentarily rivaled the brightness of the full Moon. Even from 50,000 light-years away, the radiation wave expanded and ionized Earth's upper atmosphere, causing the dead of night to briefly register daylight-level ionization. Scientists determined the magnetar rang like a titanic bell, vibrating ninety-five times a second. Had this pinpoint dead star exploded within ten light-years, its gamma-ray torrent would have stripped away Earth's protective ozone layer and unleashed planetary mass extinction.
angle: A starquake on a 12-mile-wide dead star 50,000 light-years away unleashed so much energy in 0.1 seconds that it physically warped Earth's upper atmosphere.

claims.claim: SGR 1806-20 is a magnetar, an ultradense neutron star equipped with an extreme magnetic field.
SGR 1806-20 is situated in the constellation Sagittarius on the opposite side of the Milky Way.
The giant flare from SGR 1806-20 struck Earth on December 27, 2004.
The magnetar is approximately 12 to 15 miles (20 kilometers) in diameter.
In just one-tenth of a second, the eruption released more energy than our Sun produces in over 100,000 years.
The incoming gamma rays impacted Earth's ionosphere, ionizing gas and causing the upper atmosphere to briefly expand.
In gamma rays, the explosion briefly matched or exceeded the brightness of the full Moon.
The blast was roughly 100 times more energetic than any previously recorded soft gamma repeater giant flare.
The 2004 event was the brightest extra-solar transient flash ever detected by humanity.
If a similar magnetar blast occurred within 10 light-years of Earth, it would obliterate the ozone layer and trigger mass extinction.
SGR 1806-20 rotates on its axis once every 7.5 seconds.
The magnetic field strength of SGR 1806-20 reaches around 1,000 trillion gauss (10 to the 15th power gauss).
The magnetar's magnetic field is strong enough to erase data on a credit card from halfway to the Moon.
NASA's Swift satellite detected and observed the giant flare.
The National Science Foundation's Very Large Array radio telescopes monitored the blast's aftermath.
The explosion was powered by starquake fracturing and violent magnetic reconnection in the magnetar's crust.
SGR 1806-20 belongs to the rare class of neutron stars known as soft gamma repeaters.
Only around ten to a dozen magnetars were known in our galaxy at the time of the discovery.

disputed: Distance to SGR 1806-20: S1 states 42,000 light-years (13 kiloparsecs), while S4, S5, and S7 cite approximately 50,000 light-years. Script should say 'between 40,000 and 50,000 light-years away' or 'roughly 50,000 light-years away'.

Solar equivalent energy output: S1 and S2 specify that the 0.1-second burst surpassed 150,000 years of solar output, whereas S4 and S5 state 100,000 years. Script should state 'more energy than the Sun emits in 100,000 to 150,000 years'.

Distance of the nearest known magnetar to Earth: S1 and S4 cite approximately 9,000 light-years, while S5 quotes an estimate that none are closer than 4,000 to 5,000 light-years. Attribute or use S1/S4's specific cataloged distance: 'at least several thousand light-years away'.
